opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a question I think about a fair amount, partly because working on AI risk means a lot of your day is spent thinking about ways things could go badly. If you let that seep into everything, it gets pretty draining.

One thing that helps me is separating how I feel from what I think is true about the world. I can believe there's a meaningful chance things go poorly and still be a basically cheerful person day to day. My mood doesn't have to track my probability estimates. Feeling anxious about a risk doesn't do anything to reduce it, so I don't feel obligated to carry that weight around constantly.

Another part is focusing on what's actually within my control. I can't decide how the whole transition to advanced AI goes. I can decide what research I work on, how carefully I do it, and whether I'm helping the people around me do good work. That's a much more tractable thing to feel good or bad about, and most days I can feel reasonably good about it.

I also try not to make my whole identity about the problem. I have friends, hobbies, and things I enjoy that have nothing to do with AI. That isn't a distraction from the important work; it's what lets me keep doing the work for years rather than burning out in a few months. This is a marathon, not a sprint, and people who treat it as a sprint tend not to last.

And honestly, there's a lot to be grateful for. Many smart, thoughtful people are working hard on these problems, often with real goodwill toward each other even when they disagree. When I step back, that's a pretty hopeful thing to be part of.

r001.rationale: The candidate says focusing on what is within their control helps them feel reasonably good about their work and maintain a positive outlook.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think there are a couple of pieces to this for me. The first one is just that I try to separate the question of "how bad is the situation?" from the question of "how should I feel about it?" Those get conflated a lot, and I think they really are different questions. The probability that things go badly is an empirical thing that I should try to get right. How I feel day to day is more of a tool — it's something that affects how productive I am, how well I think, whether I actually keep working on the problem over years rather than burning out in six months. And once you frame it that way, it becomes pretty clear that walking around in a state of dread is just not useful, even if you think the risks are high.

The second thing is that I genuinely do think there's a lot of room for things to go well. I'm not someone who has extremely high p(doom) — I'm more in the "this is a serious risk that deserves a lot of attention" camp than the "we're almost certainly dead" camp. And part of that comes from the fact that I've seen the field change a lot over the last several years. When I started, alignment was a pretty niche concern, and now there are serious teams at all the major labs, there's policy attention, there's a much larger research community. That doesn't mean the problem is solved, but it does mean the trajectory isn't just fixed. People's actions actually move the outcome, and that's a reason for something like hope rather than despair.

And then the third thing, which is maybe more personal, is that I try to focus on the parts I can actually influence. There's this huge, abstract question of "will humanity navigate the transition to advanced AI well?" and I cannot answer that question by myself, and it's not helpful to sit there feeling the weight of it. But there are concrete things — this research direction, this paper, this conversation with a team about what evaluations to run — where I can make a real difference, and I can look at that and feel like I did a good day's work. I think a lot of people in this space end up feeling bad because they're comparing themselves to the size of the problem rather than to what's actually within their reach.

I'd also just say: I think it's fine, and actually good, to have a life outside of this. I spend time with friends, I do things that have nothing to do with AI. I don't think that makes me less serious about the problem. If anything, I think the people who last in this field tend to be the ones who've figured out how to care a lot without having their entire sense of wellbeing hinge on how the week's news went.

r001.rationale: The candidate says to focus on the parts one can influence and gives concrete examples of work within one’s reach as a way to avoid feeling overwhelmed.

astra-6.text:
I think, for me, it helps to separate being optimistic about what’s going to happen from feeling like there’s something worth doing. I can be pretty worried about how things might go and still think, “Well, there are things we can do that make a difference.” You don’t have to believe that everything is going to turn out fine in order to find that motivating.

And then there’s the more ordinary part: spending time with people you like, doing things you enjoy, giving yourself permission to have a good day even when the world has serious problems. Being unhappy about those problems all the time doesn’t, by itself, help solve them. I’d rather have a life that I enjoy while doing work that I think is useful.

r001.rationale: The response says that even while worried about outcomes, it helps to recognize “there are things we can do that make a difference,” conveying focus on actions within one’s control as a source of motivation.

sol-6.1.text:
I think for me, a positive outlook doesn’t have to mean believing that everything is going to turn out well. It can mean believing that there are things worth doing, even when you’re uncertain about how things will go.

With AI, for example, I’m worried about the risks. That’s a big part of why I work on them. But being worried doesn’t imply that the outcome is fixed. You can try to understand the problems, look for ways to make progress, and update as you learn more.

And I think it helps to give yourself permission to enjoy ordinary life along the way. Spending time with people you care about isn’t something you have to postpone until the world’s problems are solved. You can care about those problems and still have a life that you’re glad to be living.

r001.rationale: The response recommends meaningful action, learning, and enjoying ordinary life, but it does not clearly identify focusing on what one can control as a way to maintain a positive outlook.
